title: Projects in context: standalone, programme, portfolio, customer and supplier
blurb: Describe the contexts a PRINCE2 project can sit in, from standalone to programme, portfolio and commercial, and how context shapes the method.
question: A council's street lighting project is one of six projects in its net zero programme, and an outside firm installs the lights under contract. Which contexts apply, and what do they mean for how PRINCE2 is used?

teach.body: PRINCE2 does not assume any specific organizational context. Typically there are users who specify the outputs they want (PRINCE2 calls outputs products), suppliers who provide the resources and expertise to deliver them, and business decision-makers who make sure the investment is justified and stays justified. Those parties may sit in one organization or several, and the project may stand alone or sit inside a bigger structure.

teach.caption: A project may sit in a programme, directly in a portfolio, or stand alone under a business unit's management.

teach.h: Programme and portfolio in a sentence
teach.body: A programme is a temporary structure set up to lead several related projects and other work, so that outcomes of benefit are achieved step by step. A portfolio is the whole of an organization's investment (or a segment of it) in the changes it needs to reach its strategic objectives. A project is narrower than both: one temporary organization delivering products under one agreed business case.

teach.h: Customer and supplier in a commercial context

rows.label: Why take part
values: To get the outputs and benefits

teach.caption: The project may need to align with two or more management systems, for example two quality systems.

teach.body: Larkfield County Council is replacing 9,000 street lights with low-energy units. The project is one of six in the council's net zero programme, so the programme board commissions it, sets its project tolerances and expects it to fit the programme's plan. The lights are installed by Corvane Lighting under contract. Project manager Siobhan Kerr knows Corvane has its own business case for the work, so the contract, commercial management approach and both firms' quality standards must line up.

teach.h: Context shapes the method, not the principles
teach.body: Because PRINCE2 assumes no setting, the people involved apply its principles, practices and processes to fit the context. A commercial relationship, a programme above the project or a supplier's own delivery method are all reasons to tailor. The principles themselves still apply in every context.

teach.text: PRINCE2 7 calls whoever commissions the project the BUSINESS LAYER. The 6th edition phrase 'corporate, programme management or the customer' is out of date. The business layer sits OUTSIDE the project management team, even when it is a programme.

items: PRINCE2 assumes no specific organizational context (1.5).
Typical parties: users (specify outputs), suppliers (resources and expertise), business decision-makers (justification).
A project may be standalone (reporting to a business unit) or part of a programme or portfolio (fig 1.2).
Commercial context: customer and supplier, possibly under contract; the supplier has its own business case; management systems may need aligning.
The method is applied to fit the context; the principles still apply.

summary: You can now describe the parties found in any project context and tell standalone, programme, portfolio and commercial contexts apart. You can also explain how the context shapes the way PRINCE2 is applied.

A.q: Which three types of party does PRINCE2 typically expect to find in a project's context?
options: Sponsors, contractors and regulators
Customers, auditors and team managers
Users, suppliers and business decision-makers
Users, external regulators and programme managers
A.why: PRINCE2 describes users who specify the outputs, suppliers who provide resources and expertise, and business decision-makers who ensure the investment is justified.

whyNot.0: Sponsor is not a PRINCE2 role, and regulators are not one of the typical parties described.
whyNot.1: Auditors and team managers are not the three parties PRINCE2 describes in its view of context.
whyNot.3: Users are one party, but regulators and programme managers are not the other two; suppliers and business decision-makers are.

A.q: A project reports directly to a business unit's management structure and is not part of any programme or portfolio. How is it described?
options: Standalone
Commercial
Cross-functional
Iterative
A.why: A project that reports to the business unit's management structure, outside any programme or portfolio, is a standalone project.

whyNot.1: Commercial describes a customer and supplier relationship, not where the project reports.
whyNot.2: Cross-functional is a characteristic of all projects, not a type of context.
whyNot.3: Iterative describes a delivery approach, not the organizational context.

A.q: In a commercial customer and supplier context, what does PRINCE2 say about the supplier?
options: It owns the customer's business case for the project
It provides the executive for the project board
It sets the project-level tolerances for the work
It has its own business case for taking part
A.why: In a commercial context, suppliers have their own business case for taking part, separate from the customer's business case for the project.

whyNot.0: The project's business case is owned by the executive on behalf of the business, not by the supplier.
whyNot.1: The executive represents the business interest; the supplier is represented by the senior supplier.
whyNot.2: Project-level tolerances are set by the business layer, not by the supplier.

options: The whole of an organization's investment in the changes it needs
A temporary structure leading several related projects towards outcomes
A temporary organization delivering products under one business case
A permanent unit running the organization's day-to-day operations
B.why: A programme is a temporary structure designed to lead several interrelated projects and other work so that beneficial outcomes are achieved progressively.

whyNot.0: The whole of an organization's investment in change describes a portfolio.
whyNot.2: A temporary organization delivering products under one business case is a project.
whyNot.3: A permanent unit running daily operations is business as usual.

B.q: Why might a project in a commercial context need to align two or more management systems?
options: Because the supplier must adopt the customer's systems in full
Because PRINCE2 replaces both parties' systems with its own
Because the business layer must approve each supplier task
Because customer and supplier each have their own ways of working
B.why: Customer and supplier each bring their own standards and systems (for example quality systems), so the project may need to align with two or more of them.

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 does not require the supplier to abandon its systems; it calls for them to be aligned.
whyNot.1: PRINCE2 works alongside existing systems; it does not replace them.
whyNot.2: The business layer does not approve individual supplier tasks; work is managed through work packages.

B.q:
Which two statements about projects in context are correct?
1. PRINCE2 assumes a specific organizational context.
2. A project may be part of a programme or a portfolio.
3. Suppliers in a commercial context have their own business case.
4. A standalone project does not need a business case.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: A project may sit within a programme or portfolio (statement 2), and in a commercial context suppliers have their own business case (statement 3).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is false: PRINCE2 does not assume any specific organizational context.
whyNot.2: Statements 1 and 4 are false: PRINCE2 assumes no specific context, and every PRINCE2 project needs a business case.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: every PRINCE2 project, standalone or not, needs an agreed business case.

C.q: A council's lighting project is one of six projects in its net zero programme, and an outside firm installs the lights under contract. Which two context features apply?
options: Programme and commercial
Standalone and commercial
Portfolio and internal supplier
Programme and standalone
C.why: Being one of six projects in a programme is a programme context; an outside firm working under contract makes it a commercial customer and supplier context.

whyNot.1: It is commercial, but it is not standalone because it sits within a programme.
whyNot.2: The supplier is external, under contract, so it is not an internal supplier, and the project sits in a programme.
whyNot.3: A project cannot be both standalone and within a programme.

C.q: In PRINCE2's view of context, who are the business decision-makers, and which project interest do they represent?
options: Those who specify the outputs; the user interest
Those who provide resources and skills; the supplier interest
Those who keep the investment justified; the business interest
Those who run daily operations; the operational interest
C.why: Business decision-makers ensure the investment can be justified and remains justified; they represent the business interest, led on the board by the executive.

whyNot.0: Specifying outputs is what users do, representing the user interest.
whyNot.1: Providing resources and expertise is what suppliers do, representing the supplier interest.
whyNot.3: PRINCE2's three interests are business, user and supplier; there is no operational interest.

C.q: In PRINCE2 7, what term replaces the 6th edition phrase 'corporate, programme management or the customer', and where does it sit?
options: The project board, inside the project management team
The business layer, as the directing level of the team
The executive, as the commissioning level above the board
The business layer, outside the project management team
C.why: PRINCE2 7 uses the business layer for whoever commissions the project; it sits outside the project management team, which is made up of the directing, managing and delivering levels.

whyNot.0: The project board is the directing level inside the project management team; it is not the commissioning body.
whyNot.1: The business layer is the term, but it is outside the team; the directing level is the project board.
whyNot.2: The executive is a project board role inside the project management team, not the commissioning level.

reteach.title: Think of a football club
reteach.question: A club builds a new stand. Who wants it, who builds it, who pays, and does it sit inside a bigger plan?

blocks.body: The fans and ground staff who will use the stand are the users. The construction firm is the supplier, under contract and with its own business case for the job. The club's board, which must be sure the stand pays its way, are the business decision-makers. If the stand is one of several linked projects in a 'stadium renewal' plan, it sits in a programme; if the club just builds one stand, it is standalone.

blocks.text: The builder's business case (profit from the contract) is not the club's business case (value from the stand). In a commercial context there are at least two.

explain.body: Users specify the desired outputs (products). Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver them. Business decision-makers ensure the investment can be justified and remains justified throughout the lifecycle.

test.q: In PRINCE2's view of context, which party specifies the desired outputs?
options: Suppliers
Users
Business decision-makers
Project support
test.why: Users specify the desired outputs, which PRINCE2 calls products.

whyNot.0: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the outputs.
whyNot.2: Business decision-makers ensure the investment is justified.
whyNot.3: Project support is an administrative role, not one of the parties in PRINCE2's view of context.

explain.body: A project may sit within a programme (a temporary structure leading related projects towards beneficial outcomes) or a portfolio (the organization's total investment in change), or stand alone under a business unit.

options: A temporary structure leading several related projects
A single project reporting to a business unit
The organization's total investment in the changes it needs
The set of management products held in the PID
test.why: A portfolio is the totality of an organization's investment (or a segment of it) in the changes needed to achieve its strategic objectives.

whyNot.0: A temporary structure leading related projects is a programme.
whyNot.1: A single project reporting to a business unit is a standalone project.
whyNot.3: The PID is a collection of management products for one project, not a portfolio.

explain.body: Customer and supplier may be separate organizations, often with a contract. The supplier has its own business case for taking part, and the project may need to align with two or more management systems.

test.q: Which statement about a commercial customer and supplier context is correct?
options: The supplier's business case replaces the customer's
The supplier has its own business case for taking part
The customer and supplier share a single business case
The supplier's contract removes the need for a business case
test.why: In a commercial context the supplier has its own business case for taking part, alongside the customer's business case for the project.

whyNot.0: The supplier's business case sits alongside the customer's; it does not replace it.
whyNot.2: Each party has its own business case; they are not merged into one.
whyNot.3: A contract does not remove the need for the project's business case.

explain.body: PRINCE2 assumes no context, so the people involved apply its principles, practices and processes to fit the setting. Programme links, commercial relationships and supplier methods are common reasons to tailor. The principles still apply.

test.q: How does PRINCE2 cope with projects in very different contexts?
options: The method is applied to fit the context; the principles still apply
A different version of PRINCE2 is used for each type of context
The principles are dropped where the context makes them unhelpful
The business layer rewrites the processes for each new context
test.why: PRINCE2 is designed to work in any context: the people involved apply the method to fit, while all seven principles continue to apply.

whyNot.1: There is one PRINCE2 method, applied and tailored to fit each context.
whyNot.2: The principles are not tailored away; they apply in every context.
whyNot.3: Processes are tailored by the project management team as part of applying the method, not rewritten by the business layer.
